newsitem.title: USA: Little Rock prepares Clinton victory party.
newsitem.headline: Little Rock prepares Clinton victory party.

text.p: Convinced that President Bill Clinton is heading for re-election, city officials in the capital of his home state of Arkansas are already preparing a huge election-night street party.

Little Rock city workers on Friday began closing off downtown streets around the Old State House, a large white Greek Revival structure where as many as 80,000 people are expected to gather on election night next Tuesday.
"It'll be the largest block party in Little Rock's history," said Mayor Jim Dailey, a Democrat.

When Clinton was elected president in 1992, it was on the front steps of the Old State House, which once served as the state capitol, that he claimed victory before 50,000 people. He plans to do the same again this year.

"There's some nostalgia there for the president. That's where he announced his campaign in 1991 and where he spoke after winning the following year," said Skip Rutherford, a Little Rock advertising executive and a close friend of Clinton who is helping plan the election-night events.

Dailey said many downtown merchants planned to hang bunting and keep businesses open late into election night. Virtually all 6,000 hotel rooms in metropolitan Little Rock have been reserved from Sunday night through the election.

Utility workers began days ago adding electrical circuits to handle the expected demand for power in the area around the Old State House and 500 telephone lines have been installed in an adjoining press center.

The festivities are being organized by city Democrats and the Little Rock Chamber of Commerce, a non-partisan group that sees them as a commercial opportunity rather than a political statement. But local Republicans say Clinton's allies are premature in their party plans, pointing to new polls showing that Dole is closing the gap in the last days of the campaign.
"With Dole's last-minute, 96-hour push, that may just put us over the top," said Shannon Golen, a Republican organizer in Little Rock. "It's not over until it's over."

Clinton is a polarizing figure in Arkansas. To those who back him, he is the state's favorite son and his support among blacks is rock solid. But his opponents tend to dislike him much more than those in other areas of the country.
Still, he is virtually assured of victory here. The latest opinion poll showed Clinton with 56 percent support in the state, 18 points ahead of Republican challenger Bob Dole.
On election night, hundreds of local and state police will augment the presidential Secret Service contingent, and metal detectors will be in place to help screen the crowd.

Rock stars Stephen Stills and Nicolette Larson and country singer Kathy Mattea are to play at the Riverfront Ampitheatre and TV images of the events and network election returns will be projected on huge screens throughout the downtown area.
Bars and restaurants are hiring additional staff and offering special election menus.
May Parr, a Clinton supporter who owns a popular eatery called The Blue Plate Special, said she wanted to ensure that Republicans felt comfortable in her restaurant.
"We'll be serving Dole pineapple upside down cake and, in honor of Jack Kemp, pigskin potatoes," Parr said.
